prompt: In the hierarchy, the cache is described as staging data movement between:

options.text: Registers and main memory
Main memory and secondary storage
The ALU and the control unit
Secondary and tertiary storage

explanation: The cache sits between the registers above it and main memory below it, and staging the traffic between them is its whole job.

why.a: Correct. The cache sits between the registers above it and main memory below it, and staging the traffic between them is its whole job.
why.b: Wrong. That gap is bridged by virtual memory, not by the cache.
why.c: Wrong. Both are processor units and neither is a level of the hierarchy.
why.d: Wrong. The cache is at the top of the hierarchy, not the bottom.

prompt: Select what the deck says about the cache in the hierarchy.

options.text: It stages data movement between registers and main memory
It improves performance
It is not usually visible to the processor
It is not usually visible to the programmer
It must be managed explicitly by the program

explanation: Four claims, and the last two are the important pair: the cache works without anyone asking it to. That is what makes it organizational rather than architectural.

why.a: Correct, and it is the cache's position in the hierarchy.
why.b: Correct, improving performance is the reason it exists.
why.c: Correct, not usually visible to the processor.
why.d: Correct, not usually visible to the programmer either.
why.e: Wrong, and it contradicts the two invisibility claims: a cache the program had to manage would be visible to it.

prompt: Main memory is described as:

options.text: The principal internal memory system of the computer, each location having a unique address
The fastest and smallest memory in the machine
A copy of portions of the cache
Memory that survives a power cut

explanation: Principal internal memory, with a unique address per location. That uniqueness is what makes an address field meaningful in the first place.

why.a: Correct. Principal internal memory, with a unique address per location.
why.b: Wrong. Those are registers.
why.c: Wrong, and reversed: the cache contains a copy of portions of main memory.
why.d: Wrong. Main memory is volatile; ROM and secondary storage are not.

prompt: Main memory is the principal internal memory system of the computer, and each location has a {{1}} address.
explanation: Unique. In the cache organization slides this becomes each word has a unique n-bit address.

prompt: Cache memory is designed to combine:

options.text: The access time of expensive, high-speed memory with the size of less expensive, lower-speed memory
The access time of cheap memory with the size of expensive memory
The reliability of ROM with the speed of RAM
The capacity of secondary storage with the volatility of main memory

explanation: The speed of the fast memory with the size of the slow one. It is the hierarchy's promise stated for one particular pair of levels.

why.a: Correct. The speed of the fast memory with the size of the slow one.
why.b: Wrong, and it takes the worst of each rather than the best.
why.c: Wrong. Reliability is not part of this claim.
why.d: Wrong. Volatility is not something anyone sets out to combine.

prompt: The cache contains a copy of portions of main memory.
explanation: A copy of portions, not of the whole thing. That is why a tag is needed: the cache has to record which portions it is currently holding.

why.true: Correct. Portions of main memory, copied into the cache.
why.false: Wrong. This is the deck's own description of what a cache holds.

prompt: The deck gives typical sizes as:

options.text: Cache 1 to 2 MB, main memory up to 64 GB
Cache 1 to 2 GB, main memory up to 64 MB
Cache 16 KB, main memory 128 KB
Cache 64 MB, main memory 1 to 2 GB

explanation: 1 to 2 MB against up to 64 GB, a ratio of tens of thousands to one. That gap is why the mapping functions matter.

why.a: Correct. 1 to 2 MB against up to 64 GB, a ratio of tens of thousands to one.
why.b: Wrong, and reversed, which would make the cache larger than main memory.
why.c: Wrong. Those are figures from the worked mapping examples, not the typical sizes.
why.d: Wrong on both numbers.

prompt: Cache can be 1 to 2 MB while main memory can be up to {{1}} GB.
explanation: 64 GB, against a cache of 1 to 2 MB, a ratio of tens of thousands to one.

prompt: How many bits are in a nibble and in a byte?

options.text: 4 and 8
8 and 16
2 and 8
4 and 16

explanation: A nibble is 4 bits and a byte is 8. A nibble is also exactly one hexadecimal digit, which is why hex groups bits in fours.

why.a: Correct. A nibble is 4 bits and a byte is 8.
why.b: Wrong. A byte is 8 bits, not 16.
why.c: Wrong. A nibble is 4 bits.
why.d: Wrong on the byte.

prompt: A nibble is {{1}} bits.
explanation: 4 bits, half a byte, and the origin of the name.

prompt: In the deck's memory terms, a block is:

options.text: A collection of words, typically 2, 4 or 8
A single byte
Four bits
One complete row of memory

explanation: A collection of words. The word itself is one or more complete rows of memory, and the deck's example counts 4 words to a block.

why.a: Correct. A collection of words.
why.b: Wrong. A byte is 8 bits.
why.c: Wrong. Four bits is a nibble.
why.d: Wrong. That is the deck's definition of a word.

prompt: A word is one or more complete {{1}} of memory.
explanation: Rows. The slide draws memory as a grid, so a row is the natural unit and a block is several of them.

prompt: A memory size of 4 MB works out as how many bits?
explanation: 4 times 1024 times 1024 gives 4,194,304 bytes, and multiplying by 8 gives 33,554,432 bits.

why.a: Correct. 4 times 1024 times 1024 gives 4,194,304 bytes, and multiplying by 8 gives 33,554,432 bits.
why.b: Wrong. That is the answer in bytes, before multiplying by 8.
why.c: Wrong. It uses 1000 rather than 1024 and skips the bits conversion.
why.d: Wrong. 81,920 bits is the deck's figure for 10 KB.

prompt: 10 KB works out as 10 times 1024 times 8, which is {{1}} bits.
explanation: 81,920 bits. The two steps are always the same: to bytes with 1024, then to bits with 8.

prompt: When the processor attempts to read a word and the word is in the cache, this is called a cache hit. What happens?

options.text: The word is delivered to the processor
The block containing it is read into the cache first
The address is loaded onto the system bus
The cache line is updated with a new tag

explanation: Straight delivery, with no main memory traffic at all. The other three options all describe what happens on a miss.

why.a: Correct. Straight delivery, with no main memory traffic at all.
why.b: Wrong. That is the miss path.
why.c: Wrong. On a hit the data and address buffers are disabled and there is no bus traffic.
why.d: Wrong. Updating the line with a new tag happens on a miss.

prompt: When the processor attempts to read a word of memory, a check is made to determine if the word is in the {{1}}.
explanation: The cache. That check happens on every read, which is why the deck later notes it is being ignored for simplicity in the two-level calculation.

prompt: On a cache miss, what is read into the cache?

options.text: The block of main memory that contains the word
The single word only
The whole page containing the word
Nothing, the word is read straight from main memory

explanation: The whole block, not just the word. Spatial locality says the neighbours will be wanted soon, so fetching them is not waste.

why.a: Correct, and the cache then delivers the word to the processor.
why.b: Wrong, and it would throw away the benefit of spatial locality.
why.c: Wrong. Pages belong to virtual memory, blocks to the cache.
why.d: Wrong. The deck's sequence loads the block first.

prompt: On a cache {{1}}, the block of main memory containing the word is read into the cache, and the cache then delivers the {{2}} to the processor.
explanation: A miss brings in a block, but only a word is handed to the processor.

prompt: Because of the locality of reference principle, when a block of data is fetched into the cache:

options.text: It is likely that there will be future references to that same memory location
It is unlikely to be referenced again
It must be written back immediately
It replaces the entire cache

explanation: Future references are likely, by both temporal and spatial locality. Without that likelihood, caching would be a pure cost.

why.a: Correct. Future references are likely, by both temporal and spatial locality.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the exact opposite of the locality principle.
why.c: Wrong. Write-back timing is not discussed here.
why.d: Wrong. A block replaces a line, not the whole cache.

prompt: The justification for reading a whole block into the cache is the locality of reference principle, in both its time and space forms.
explanation: The deck cites locality of reference, time and space, at exactly this point. Space justifies fetching the neighbours, time justifies keeping them.

why.true: Correct. The slide names both forms as the reason.
why.false: Wrong. Locality is precisely the principle the deck appeals to here.

prompt: How does the deck describe L2 cache relative to L1?

options.text: Slower and typically larger
Faster and typically smaller
The same speed but larger
Slower and typically smaller

explanation: Slower and larger, and L3 stands in the same relation to L2. The whole hierarchy repeats inside the cache.

why.a: Correct. Slower and larger, and L3 stands in the same relation to L2.
why.b: Wrong, and reversed.
why.c: Wrong. It is slower as well as larger.
why.d: Wrong. It is larger, not smaller.

prompt: L3 cache is {{1}} and typically {{2}} than the L2 cache.
explanation: Slower and larger, exactly as L2 is to L1.

prompt: Main memory consists of 2 to the power n addressable words. What follows about each word's address?

options.text: Each word has a unique n-bit address
Each word has a unique 2n-bit address
Addresses are shared between blocks
Each block, not each word, has an address

explanation: n bits address 2 to the power n words, one address each. It is the same counting argument as the unsigned range.

why.a: Correct. N bits address 2 to the power n words, one address each.
why.b: Wrong. 2n bits would address 2 to the power 2n words.
why.c: Wrong. The addresses are unique.
why.d: Wrong. Words are addressable; blocks are groups of words.

prompt: Memory consists of a number of fixed-length blocks of {{1}} words each.
explanation: K words per block. M is the number of blocks, m is the number of cache lines, and n is the address width, so the four letters are worth keeping straight.

prompt: How many blocks does main memory contain?

options.text: M equals 2 to the power n, divided by K
M equals 2 to the power n, times K
M equals K divided by 2 to the power n
M equals 2 to the power K, divided by n

explanation: Total words over words per block. The same shape appears in the worked examples as cache size over line size.

why.a: Correct. Total words over words per block.
why.b: Wrong. Multiplying would give more blocks than words.
why.c: Wrong, and it inverts the division.
why.d: Wrong. The exponent is n, and K is the divisor.

prompt: If main memory holds 2 to the power n words in blocks of K words, the number of blocks is 2 to the power n divided by K.
explanation: It is, and the deck writes it as M equals 2 to the power n over K.

why.true: Correct. Total words divided by words per block.
why.false: Wrong. This is the formula given directly on the slide.

prompt: Cache memory consists of m blocks, which are called:

options.text: Lines
Pages
Frames
Segments

explanation: Lines, each containing K words, the same K as a main memory block. The worked examples treat block size, frame size and line size as the same quantity.

why.a: Correct, and line is the word the mapping functions use throughout.
why.b: Wrong. Pages belong to virtual memory.
why.c: Wrong here, although the worked examples note that frame size means the same as line size.
why.d: Wrong. Segment is the pipelining deck's word for a stage.

prompt: Each cache line contains K words and also includes {{1}} bits.
explanation: Control bits, which the deck notes are not shown in its figure. The tag is held alongside them.

prompt: If a word in a block of memory is read, what is transferred to a cache line?

options.text: The whole block
The word alone
The tag alone
The whole page

explanation: The block. That is the unit of transfer between main memory and the cache, and it is why the block size fixes the offset field width.

why.a: Correct. The block.
why.b: Wrong. Transferring one word would waste the fetch and ignore spatial locality.
why.c: Wrong. The tag identifies the block; it is not the payload.
why.d: Wrong. Pages are the unit of virtual memory, not of cache transfer.

prompt: If a word in a block of memory is read, the whole {{1}} is transferred to a cache line.
explanation: Block. Main memory is divided into blocks and the cache into lines, and a block occupies a line.

prompt: Because m is much less than M, the cache cannot permanently store a block. What follows?

options.text: It needs to identify the block currently stored, and that information is held in the tag field
It must store every block in turn
It must be flushed after each instruction
Blocks must be smaller than lines

explanation: Far more blocks than lines, so any line could be holding one of many blocks. The tag is what says which.

why.a: Correct, and it is the reason the tag field exists at all.
why.b: Wrong. Storing every block would need a cache the size of main memory.
why.c: Wrong. Flushing on a context switch is a virtual cache issue, not this one.
why.d: Wrong. A block occupies a line, so they are the same size.

prompt: The information identifying which block a cache line is holding is stored in the {{1}} field.
explanation: The tag field. Every mapping function in the next topic is really a question about how wide that field has to be.

prompt: In the cache read operation, what does the processor generate first?

options.text: The read address, RA, of the word to be read
The tag of the block
The line number
The block offset

explanation: The read address RA. The tag, index and offset are then extracted from it by the cache hardware.

why.a: Correct. The read address RA.
why.b: Wrong. The tag is a part of the address, derived from it afterwards.
why.c: Wrong. The line number is also a field within the address.
why.d: Wrong. The offset is likewise a field within the address.

prompt: The processor generates the read address, abbreviated {{1}}, of the word to be read.
explanation: RA. Do not confuse it with EA, the effective address of the addressing modes topic, or with MAR, the register that holds an address.

prompt: On a miss, the block is loaded into the cache and the word is delivered to the processor. How do these two operations relate?

options.text: They occur in parallel
The load must finish before the delivery starts
The delivery must finish before the load starts
Only one of the two happens

explanation: In parallel, which is what stops the processor waiting for the whole block to arrive before it can use the word it asked for.

why.a: Correct, and the deck says these last two operations occur in parallel.
why.b: Wrong, and it would waste time.
why.c: Wrong, and it reverses the order as well.
why.d: Wrong. Both happen.

prompt: On a cache miss, loading the block into the cache and delivering the word to the processor happen one after the other, never at the same time.
explanation: They occur in parallel. The deck says so explicitly at the end of the cache read operation.

why.true: Wrong. The slide states that these last two operations occur in parallel.
why.false: Correct. They overlap, which is what keeps the miss penalty down.

prompt: The cache connects to the processor via which lines?

options.text: Data
Control
Address
Interrupt

explanation: Data, control and address, the same three kinds of line the system buses carry.

why.a: Correct, data lines.
why.b: Correct, control lines.
why.c: Correct, address lines.
why.d: Wrong. Interrupt lines are not mentioned in this course.

prompt: The data and address lines also attach to data and address buffers, which attach to:

options.text: A system bus, from which main memory is reached
The register file
The control unit
Secondary storage directly

explanation: The system bus, and main memory lies beyond it. That path is what a cache hit avoids using.

why.a: Correct. The system bus, and main memory lies beyond it.
why.b: Wrong. The register file sits inside the processor.
why.c: Wrong. The control unit generates control signals rather than receiving the buffers.
why.d: Wrong. Secondary storage is not part of this diagram.

prompt: When a cache hit occurs, what happens to the data and address buffers?

options.text: They are disabled, so communication is only between processor and cache and there is no system bus traffic
They are enabled, so the address goes onto the system bus
They are flushed
They forward the request to main memory anyway

explanation: Disabled, and no system bus traffic. That silence on the bus is the real saving of a cache hit.

why.a: Correct. Disabled, and no system bus traffic.
why.b: Wrong. That is what happens on a miss.
why.c: Wrong. Flushing is what a virtual cache does on a context switch.
why.d: Wrong. There would be no point in a cache that always asked main memory too.

prompt: On a cache hit there is no system {{1}} traffic.
explanation: No system bus traffic. Communication stays between the processor and the cache.

prompt: When a cache miss occurs, the desired address is loaded onto the system bus and the data are returned through the data buffer to:

options.text: Both the cache and the processor
The cache only
The processor only
Main memory

explanation: Both at once, which is the parallel loading and delivering described in the cache read operation.

why.a: Correct. Both at once, which is the parallel loading and delivering described in the cache read operation.
why.b: Wrong. The processor gets its word at the same time.
why.c: Wrong. The cache keeps a copy, otherwise the next reference would miss again.
why.d: Wrong. Main memory is where the data came from.

prompt: On a cache miss the desired address is loaded onto the system bus.
explanation: It is, because main memory can only be reached across the bus. On a hit the buffers stay disabled and the bus stays quiet.

why.true: Correct. The miss path goes out over the system bus.
why.false: Wrong. That is exactly what distinguishes a miss from a hit in the deck's account.

topic: the two types of cache address
prompt: The two types of cache address are:

options.text: Physical addresses, the actual memory addresses, and logical addresses, the virtual-memory addresses
Tag addresses and index addresses
Absolute addresses and relative addresses
Read addresses and write addresses

explanation: Physical and logical. A cache using logical addresses is a virtual cache, which the deck then compares against the alternative.

why.a: Correct. Physical and logical.
why.b: Wrong. Tag and index are fields within an address, not kinds of address.
why.c: Wrong. Relative addressing is an addressing mode.
why.d: Wrong. Direction of access is not what distinguishes them.

topic: the two types of cache address
prompt: Match each type of cache address to what it is.
explanation: Physical means real, logical means virtual. The mapping between them is what virtual memory performs.

prompt: Virtual memory performs mapping between:

options.text: The logical addresses used by a program and physical addresses
Cache lines and main memory blocks
Registers and cache lines
Instructions and data

explanation: Logical to physical. Its main idea is to let a program disregard the amount of main memory available.

why.a: Correct. Logical to physical.
why.b: Wrong. That mapping is the cache mapping function.
why.c: Wrong. No such mapping is described in this course.
why.d: Wrong. Separating instructions from data is the Harvard architecture.

prompt: The main idea behind virtual memory is to {{1}} the amount of main memory available.
explanation: Disregard it. The program is written as though memory were unlimited, and the mapping deals with the truth.

prompt: A virtual cache stores data using logical addresses. What follows for the processor?

options.text: It accesses the cache directly, without going through the MMU
It must go through the MMU on every access
It cannot use the cache for writes
It must flush the cache on every access

explanation: Straight to the cache, with no address translation first. Skipping the MMU is exactly where the speed comes from.

why.a: Correct. Straight to the cache, with no address translation first.
why.b: Wrong, and it would remove the advantage.
why.c: Wrong. Nothing here restricts writes.
why.d: Wrong. Flushing is needed at a context switch, not on every access.

prompt: A virtual cache stores data using {{1}} addresses.
explanation: Logical, which is the same thing as virtual-memory addresses.

topic: the advantage of a virtual cache
prompt: The advantage of a virtual cache is:

options.text: Faster access speed, since the cache can respond without an MMU address translation
Lower cost per bit
Greater capacity
No need to flush on a context switch

explanation: Speed, because a translation step is removed from the path.

why.a: Correct. Speed, because a translation step is removed from the path.
why.b: Wrong. The addressing scheme does not change the cost of the memory.
why.c: Wrong. Capacity is unaffected.
why.d: Wrong, and precisely backwards: flushing on a context switch is its disadvantage.

topic: the advantage of a virtual cache
prompt: A virtual cache is faster because it can respond without needing an MMU address translation.
explanation: That is the stated advantage. The translation is real work, and skipping it saves time on every hit.

why.true: Correct. Faster access speed, with no MMU translation required.
why.false: Wrong. This is the advantage the deck gives for the virtual cache.

topic: the disadvantage of a virtual cache
prompt: What is the disadvantage of a virtual cache?

options.text: The same virtual address in two applications refers to two different physical addresses, so the cache must be flushed at each context switch, or extra bits added to each line
It cannot hold instructions, only data
It is slower than a physical cache
It requires an MMU translation on every access

explanation: Two programs can use the same virtual address for different real data, so the cache has to be emptied between them, or each line must record which address space it belongs to.

why.a: Correct, and the deck gives both remedies.
why.b: Wrong. There is no such restriction.
why.c: Wrong. Speed is its advantage.
why.d: Wrong, and that is exactly what it avoids.

topic: the disadvantage of a virtual cache
prompt: Either the virtual cache must be {{1}} with each application context switch, or extra bits must be added to each cache line to identify which virtual address {{2}} the address refers to.
explanation: Flushed, and virtual address space. Two remedies for one problem: throw the contents away, or label them.

prompt: Cache size should be small enough that, and large enough that:

options.text: The overall average cost per bit is close to that of main memory alone, and the overall average access time is close to that of the cache alone
The average cost per bit is close to that of the cache alone, and the average access time is close to that of main memory alone
Both cost and access time match main memory
Both cost and access time match the cache

explanation: Pay like main memory, perform like cache. Which side each of the two words attaches to is the whole trick of this sentence.

why.a: Correct. Pay like main memory, perform like cache.
why.b: Wrong, and it swaps the two, which would give the worst of both.
why.c: Wrong. Matching main memory's access time would make the cache pointless.
why.d: Wrong. Matching the cache's cost per bit would be unaffordable.

prompt: The cache should be small enough that the average cost per bit is close to that of {{1}} alone, and large enough that the average access time is close to that of {{2}} alone.
explanation: Cost like main memory, speed like the cache. Cache is dear and fast, so being small keeps the cost down and being large keeps the hit rate up.

prompt: Why do large caches tend to be slightly slower than small ones?

options.text: The larger the cache, the more complex the addressing logic
Larger caches use cheaper memory technology
Larger caches must be flushed more often
Larger caches have a lower hit rate

explanation: More complex addressing logic. It is a real limit on how far the size cure can be taken, and available chip and board area limits it further.

why.a: Correct. More complex addressing logic.
why.b: Wrong. The technology is not what changes with size here.
why.c: Wrong. Flushing relates to virtual caches and context switches.
why.d: Wrong. A larger cache generally has a better hit rate, which is why anyone would want one.

prompt: Besides the addressing logic, available {{1}} and board area also limits cache size.
explanation: Chip and board area. A cache has to physically fit, which is a hard limit no design cleverness removes.
